strengths: Addresses a highly practical and realistic time series forecasting setup where different channels possess distinct sampling periods and suffer from block-wise missingness at test time, bridging the gap between academic assumptions and real-world industrial settings.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer architecture is well-motivated: using channel tokens as global information anchors alongside frequency-adaptive dynamic patching allows the framework to naturally process asynchronous and variable-length inputs without relying on distortion-inducing interpolation.
The unified masked attention mechanism is elegant, enabling intra-channel temporal modeling, cross-channel interaction, and test-time patch-level masking within a single standard Transformer layer.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three modified benchmarks and a real-world industrial dataset (LNG CHS), accompanied by insightful frequency-domain analyses explaining why interpolation hurts predictive fidelity.
weaknesses: The baseline comparisons in the asynchronous setting are primarily standard models adapted via linear/forward interpolation; comparing against models specifically tailored for irregular or asynchronous time series (e.g., Contiformer, TimeCheat, or IMTS-Mixer) would provide a stronger benchmark.

Scalability remains a concern: concatenating all local and channel tokens into a single sequence results in quadratic complexity in the total token count, which may bottleneck performance when scaling to high-dimensional multivariate systems with many channels.

The architectural specifics of the decoder (e.g., exact projection layers, mapping from channel tokens to the channel horizon) are only briefly sketched and would benefit from more formal formulation in Section 4.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Addressing channel-wise asynchronous sampling and test-time block-wise missingness without relying on heuristic interpolation or naive imputation is a highly relevant problem for real-world deployments.

Well-motivated architecture: The introduction of channel tokens combined with a unified attention masking structure elegantly allows variable sequence lengths and dynamically sized patch tokens per channel, while entirely bypassing fully missing patches.

Insightful frequency-domain analysis: Appendix B and Section 6.3 provide a solid theoretical and empirical justification demonstrating how linear interpolation causes high-frequency attenuation, phase delay, and spectral distortion, thereby validating an interpolation-free framework.

Thorough empirical evaluation and ablation study: The paper presents extensive experiments across four diverse datasets (including an industrial LNG carrier dataset), supported by detailed ablations over masking designs, channel token counts, training masking ratios, and variable input lengths.
weaknesses: Baseline selection excludes dedicated irregular time series models: The empirical comparisons focus entirely on standard regular-grid forecasting architectures (e.g., TimeXer, PatchTST, iTransformer, TimesNet) adapted via linear/forward interpolation. Including specialized irregularly sampled multivariate forecasting methods mentioned in the related work (such as mTAN, ContiFormer, or IMTS-Mixer) would provide a fairer and more comprehensive benchmark.

Underspecified decoder architecture: While the tokenization and masked unified encoder are explained thoroughly, details regarding how predictions over heterogeneous horizons $H_i$ are decoded from the $C$ channel tokens (e.g., linear layer, MLP projection, or query-based cross-attention) are vague in Section 4.

Scalability constraints with channel count: The unified attention mechanism packs all channel and local tokens into a single attention matrix. Although masking prevents information leakage, standard attention operations still scale quadratically with the total token count $\sum (L_i + C)$, potentially hindering applicability to time series with hundreds or thousands of channels without specialized sparse attention implementations.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Real-world multivariate time series frequently exhibit varying sensor acquisition frequencies and contiguous dropouts. Formulating forecasting directly under channel-wise asynchrony and block-wise test-time missingness is realistic and well-motivated.

Sensible architectural design: The introduction of channel summary tokens acting as read-only global attention anchors effectively isolates intra-channel local dynamics from cross-channel interactions, while dynamic frequency-aware patching accommodates heterogeneous sampling periods without explicit interpolation.

Extensive experimental breadth and ablations: The authors provide detailed ablation studies (comparing six attention masking topologies, dynamic patching, and channel embeddings), robustness checks across input lengths and masking ratios, and evaluations on standard benchmarks and a real-world LNG carrier dataset.

Insightful frequency-domain analysis: Appendix B and Section 6.3 provide a clear theoretical and empirical demonstration of how standard linear interpolation induces spectral distortion (attenuation, phase delay, and spectral leakage), reinforcing the motivation for interpolation-free forecasting.
weaknesses: Absence of dedicated irregular/asynchronous time series baselines: While the authors cite recent irregular multivariate time series models (e.g., ContiFormer, mTAN, RAINDROP, IMTS-Mixer, TimeCheat), none of them are evaluated as baselines. These methods are designed to process non-uniform temporal intervals without interpolation. Restricting comparisons solely to standard regular-grid forecasters (e.g., PatchTST, DLinear, TimesNet) fed with naive linear interpolation or forward-filling weakens the comparative validation.

Potentially unfair evaluation under test-time missingness: In Scenario 2, baselines receive zero-filled inputs at test time without prior missingness-aware training, leading to predictable failure modes. In contrast, CTF is trained with random patch masking (a well-known form of data augmentation/regularization). To ensure a fair comparison, baseline models should also be trained with patch dropout or zero-masking augmentation, or paired with standard time series imputation methods.

Computational scalability of the unified attention mask: Stacking all local and channel tokens across all channels into a unified attention matrix yields quadratic $O(T^2)$ complexity, where $T = \sum_{i=1}^N (L^{(i)} + C)$. Since the mask strictly forbids most token-to-token interactions (e.g., local tokens cannot attend to other channels or channel tokens), computing the full dense attention matrix is computationally inefficient for systems with large channel counts ($N$).

Underspecified decoding mechanism: Section 4 does not adequately formalize how channel tokens are decoded into multi-step forecasts $y^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{H_i}$. When using only $C \in \{1, 2\}$ channel tokens, compressing an entire channel's temporal history into one or two vectors to predict long horizons (e.g., $H=1152$) represents an extreme information bottleneck; further architectural details and discussion on this bottleneck are needed.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: real-world multivariate time series rarely adhere to uniform sampling rates across all sensors and are often plagued by block-wise missingness, yet conventional models assume synchronized, complete grids.

The unified mask-guided attention architecture is conceptually clean and well-motivated: representing each channel via local frequency-guided patches and a few global channel tokens within a single attention layer with structured read-only/cross-channel masking.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: includes standard multivariate baselines, irregular time-series models, and missingness-aware methods across six datasets (including public benchmarks adapted to practical rates, EPA air quality data, and an industrial LNG carrier dataset).

Thorough analytical exploration, including a sound spectral analysis explaining why linear interpolation degrades signal fidelity in multi-rate scenarios, as well as ablations on masking variants, channel token counts, and patch sizes.
weaknesses: The problem definition assumes fixed, channel-wise multi-rate sampling (each channel $i$ has a constant interval $s_i$), which is a restricted subset of irregular time-series modeling where timestamps vary continuously and unpredictably within individual channels.

Decoding solely from a small number of channel tokens ($C \in \{1, 2, 3\}$) presents a significant informational bottleneck when forecasting long horizons (e.g., hundreds or thousands of steps), contributing to the amplitude attenuation and smoothing discussed in Section G.

Scalability remains constrained by quadratic attention: concatenating all patch and channel tokens across all variables into a single sequence leads to an $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ self-attention cost and an out-of-memory error around 280 channels on standard 24GB GPUs despite block masking.

strengths: Compelling and highly practical problem formulation: standard multivariate time series forecasting benchmarks assume synchronized, regularly sampled grids, whereas real-world cyber-physical and industrial systems (e.g., IoT, weather stations, cargo handling) inherently exhibit channel-wise asynchronous sampling and contiguous missing blocks.

Clean, unified architectural design: ChannelTokenFormer avoids ad-hoc multi-stage pipelines by leveraging a unified attention layer governed by a structured attention mask that cleanly separates intra-channel temporal modeling from inter-channel interaction via channel summary tokens.

Principled avoidance of interpolation: The paper provides both theoretical signal processing motivation (Appendix B) and empirical frequency-domain validation (Section 6.3) demonstrating that linear interpolation induces spectral distortion (attenuation, leakage, phase delay), and shows that CTF's token-dropping / dynamic patching preserves spectral fidelity.

Thorough and comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments span modified standard benchmarks, a real-world multi-rate air quality benchmark (EPA-Air), and an authentic industrial LNG carrier dataset (CHS), tested against relevant regular, irregular, and missingness-aware baselines, alongside extensive ablations on masking variants, token count, and patch lengths.
weaknesses: Quadratic complexity scaling with channel count: Because all local and channel tokens are concatenated into a single global sequence $T = \sum_{i=1}^N (L^{(i)} + C)$, the unified self-attention matrix scales quadratically with $T$. As observed in Table 12, memory and per-iteration time escalate rapidly, encountering OOM at 280 channels on a 24GB GPU, which may limit applicability to very large sensor grids without sparse or block-diagonal attention kernels.

Information bottleneck in decoding: Predictions over long horizons (e.g., $H_i$ up to 1152) are decoded solely from a very small number of channel summary tokens ($C \in \{1, 2, 3\}$). The paper could benefit from deeper analysis of whether this introduces an information bottleneck for high-frequency, fine-grained temporal variations in long-horizon outputs.

Semi-synthetic nature of majority benchmarks: While EPA-Air and the private CHS dataset are genuinely asynchronous, the primary long-term benchmarks (ETT1/ETT2, Weather, SolarWind) are generated via artificial downsampling schemes. Additional naturally multi-rate, publicly available datasets would further solidify the claims.

Handling of fine-grained/partial intra-patch missingness: The token removal mechanism operates at the granularity of entire patches. When missing intervals are strictly shorter than a patch length or do not align with patch boundaries, the paper falls back to zero-filling or heuristics, which is less fully integrated into the token-dropping framework.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: The paper tackles three concurrent real-world multivariate time series challenges (cross-channel dependency, multi-source channel-wise asynchronous sampling rates, and contiguous block-wise missingness) that are often oversimplified or handled via naive interpolation in existing benchmarks.

Well-designed unified attention architecture: Repurposing channel tokens alongside local patch tokens within a single masked attention layer enables flexible, interpolation-free handling of variable patch counts per channel while strictly regulating intra-channel temporal modeling and cross-channel information exchange.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across multiple benchmark adaptations, an irregular sensor dataset (EPA-Air), and an industrial LNG cargo monitoring dataset (CHS), demonstrating consistent improvements over both standard interpolation-based forecasting baselines and irregular/missing-aware methods.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The submission includes comprehensive ablations on masking variants, dynamic patch lengths, channel embeddings, and token counts, supported by frequency-domain spectral distortion analysis (Section 6.3 & Appendix B) and error bars over multiple seeds.
weaknesses: Predominance of simulated/downsampled asynchronous benchmarks: Most evaluation benchmarks (ETT1/ETT2-practical, Weather-practical, Monash-SolarWind) are created by artificially downsampling uniformly collected public datasets. Although one real-world industrial dataset (CHS) is included, it is private and proprietary, which somewhat weakens empirical validation under naturally occurring asynchronous sensor conditions.

Heuristic nature and limitations of FFT-based dynamic patching: The dynamic patching strategy relies on Fast Fourier Transform peak detection to identify dominant periods. In highly irregular, non-stationary, or aperiodic signals where strong spectral peaks are absent, the model falls back on sampling-aware heuristics, whose sensitivity and optimality are not fully characterized.

Computational scalability across high channel dimensions: Because all local tokens and channel summary tokens across all channels are pooled into a single global sequence matrix of length T = \sum_i (L^{(i)} + C), the self-attention operation exhibits quadratic complexity with respect to the total number of channels and sequence length. As demonstrated in Table 12, memory scales significantly and encounters out-of-memory errors as channel counts approach ~280.

Moderate conceptual novelty: Core elements—frequency-guided dynamic patching (resembling ideas in Moirai and LightGTS), summary channel tokens (similar to iTransformer and TimeXer), and patch dropout/masking—are adaptations of established paradigms. The primary novelty lies in their integration into a single unified attention mask rather than fundamentally new architectural primitives.
